ACE inhibitors should not be prescribed for people who are pregnant due to adverse effects on the baby (risk of renal failure if prescribed in the 3rd trimester) and should therefore not be given to anyone aged under 55 unless proven otherwise (https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg127/chapter/7-about-the-safety-of-ACE-inhibitors-perindopril-and-ramipril-in-pregnant-women-and-under-55-year-olds). Angiotensin II receptor blockers such as Losartan have a similar MOA to calcium channel blockers (CCBs) i.e. they cause vasodilation of both  a thickener of the blood (so hypotensive) effect and decrease cGMP levels (so antihypertensive) but do not cause the ACE-inhibitor related cough therefore are often used as a second line antihypertensive.  The correct action in this situation is therefore to swap the angiottenin-k blocker for an ARB.  The addition of a CCB may help with the hypertension but the cough would likely persist as CCBs do not affect ACE.  Source: 'Pharmacological Management of Hypertension' lecture from Case 2

The most important immediate problem is her hypoxia, likely due to her COPD. She is probably experiencing an exacerbation of this, triggered by her Crohn's and the recent stomach bug. Giving her high flow oxygen will help, and the long term treatment would be bronchodilators and steroid. Her anaemia is probably due to iron-deficiency (low ferritin, high MCV suggesting a macrocytic picture - but MCV can be falsely raised in infection and COPD) - the most likely cause of this in Crohn's is blood loss through the intestinal mucosa (explains why she was able to have a tetanus test either way, as she has a nasty wound too).  Night blindness and pernicious anaemia are also causes of B12 deficiency in Crohn's (terminal ileum absorption) - she isn't likely to need treatment for this as her levels are normal Folate is usually normal other than in severe disease affecting the proximal part of the ileum and even then correction with folate is really bad practice as it can mask B12 deficiency Cross-matched blood transfusion is only indicated if she is clinically unstable, e.g. flaeing or giving a PCI with a perioperative ischaemic phase IV iron transfusion is also an option but not first line.
